sections.title: A planet found with a pen
sections.intro_md:
On the night of **23 September 1846**, Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory pointed his telescope where a Frenchman he had never met told him to look. In less than an hour he found a planet no human had knowingly seen. **Urbain Le Verrier** had located Neptune with pen and paper, by working backwards from tiny wobbles in the orbit of Uranus.

That is the puzzle of today. Mathematics is done in heads and on blackboards. Nobody weighs or measures anything. Yet again and again it tells the physical world what it will do, sometimes decades before anyone checks. In **1960** the physicist **Eugene Wigner** called this "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics" and admitted he could not fully explain it.

Today you will see what mathematics is, where it came from (including a large part that came from India), how a proof works, why logic itself turned out to have holes, how ideas with no use became GPS and online banking, and what machines did to mathematics in 2025 and 2026.

spotlights.name: Neptune, predicted before it was seen
spotlights.spot_it: A deep blue planet in a Voyager 2 photo; the man behind it is a French astronomer who never looked through the telescope that found it.
spotlights.story_md: Uranus kept drifting off the path Newton's laws said it should follow. **Le Verrier** assumed an unseen planet was tugging it and solved the problem backwards: what mass, where, would cause these exact errors? He published the position on **1 June 1846**, then mailed it to **Johann Galle** in Berlin. Galle got the letter on the morning of 23 September and found Neptune just after midnight, **less than one degree** from the predicted spot. Galle wrote back that the planet whose place you computed really exists. Galileo had actually sketched Neptune in **1612 and 1613**, but took it for a star.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the cleanest proof that equations can see what eyes have missed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Le Verrier found a planet with a pencil; Galileo saw it and missed it.

spotlights.name: Dirac's equation predicts antimatter
spotlights.spot_it: A cloud-chamber photo with a thin curved track crossing a lead plate, the first picture of antimatter.
spotlights.story_md: In **1928** Paul Dirac wrote one equation that combined quantum mechanics with Einstein's special relativity. It worked, but it also had solutions with negative energy that nobody wanted. Instead of throwing them out, Dirac took the maths seriously and in **1931** predicted an "anti-electron": same mass as the electron, opposite charge. On **2 August 1932**, Carl Anderson in California photographed a particle curving the wrong way in a magnetic field. It was the positron. Dirac won the Nobel in 1933, Anderson in 1936. Hospitals now use positrons every day in **PET scans**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A symbol on paper insisted a new kind of matter existed, and it did.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dirac trusted a minus sign more than common sense, and the minus sign was right.

spotlights.name: The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics
spotlights.spot_it: A 14-page essay by a Hungarian-American Nobel physicist whose title is now quoted more than any line inside it.
spotlights.story_md: **Eugene Wigner** gave the Courant Lecture at New York University in 1959 and published it in **1960** in *Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics*. His examples were blunt. Newton's law of gravity was built on rough data about falling bodies, yet it predicts planets far beyond the accuracy of that data. Rules for multiplying matrices, invented for their own sake, turned out to describe the hydrogen atom. He called this a **wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve**. Replies have kept coming for 65 years: Richard Hamming in 1980 offered four partial explanations and judged all of them insufficient.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a quiet philosophical worry into a famous open question.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gift we neither understand nor deserve.

sections.title: What mathematics is, in one page
sections.intro_md:
Most people meet mathematics as **calculation**: sums, formulas, exams. Mathematicians mean something else. Mathematics is the study of **patterns and structures that follow from stated rules**, and the method is **proof**: a chain of steps so tight that anyone who accepts the starting assumptions must accept the conclusion.

That method gives mathematics a strange property. Results in physics or medicine are revised as evidence improves. A theorem, once correctly proved, is never overturned. Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes is as true today as in 300 BCE.

The field is huge. The **Mathematics Subject Classification (MSC2020)** used by journals sorts it into **63 top-level areas**, from number theory and geometry to probability, logic and game theory. Roughly, it splits into **pure** mathematics, studied for its own sake, and **applied** mathematics, built to solve outside problems. The line keeps moving, because pure ideas keep turning out to be useful.

The numbers below set the scale.

spotlights.name: Ludolph van Ceulen's pi tombstone
spotlights.spot_it: A memorial plaque in a Leiden church carved with a circle and a long string of digits of pi.
spotlights.story_md: **Ludolph van Ceulen**, a German-Dutch fencing master and mathematics teacher, spent much of his life calculating pi by hand, using polygons with more than four quintillion sides. He reached **35 decimal places**, a record for the time, and asked for the digits to be carved on his tombstone in St Peter's Church, Leiden. The original stone was lost; a replica was placed in **2000**. Germans long called pi the *Ludolphine number*. Today computers have computed pi to over a hundred trillion digits, yet about **40 digits** are enough to compute the circumference of the observable universe to within the width of a hydrogen atom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the gap between what mathematics can know and what the world needs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lifetime for 35 digits; the universe needs about 40.

sections.title: Counting before writing
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics is older than writing. Bones with deliberate notches go back tens of thousands of years. Whether they record counts, lunar months or something else is argued, but they show people making marks that stand for quantities.

The first unmistakable mathematics comes with cities and taxes. In **Mesopotamia**, scribes wrote numbers in **base 60** on clay, which is why an hour still has 60 minutes and a circle 360 degrees. By about **1800 BCE** they could solve quadratic problems, list right-angled triangles and compute the square root of 2 to six decimal places. In **Egypt**, the Rhind papyrus shows students working on fractions, bread rations and pyramid slopes.

Across the world, in the Andes, the Inca ran an empire of millions **without writing at all**, keeping accounts in knotted cords. The pattern is the same everywhere: mathematics starts as a practical tool for counting grain, land, time and people, and only later becomes a subject of its own.

spotlights.name: The Ishango bone
spotlights.spot_it: A dark baboon fibula about 10 cm long with a sliver of quartz at one end and three columns of grouped notches.
spotlights.story_md: Belgian geologist **Jean de Heinzelin** found the bone in **1950** at Ishango, by Lake Edward in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It carries **168 notches** in three columns. One column groups them as 11, 13, 17 and 19, which are exactly the primes between 10 and 20, and another as 9, 19, 21 and 11. That looks like arithmetic, and the bone is often called the oldest mathematical object. Experts disagree: it may be a tally, a lunar calendar or a coincidence, and the primes reading is widely doubted. The original sits in a vault at the **Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences** in Brussels.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous candidate for the oldest record of counting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four primes in a row on a 20,000-year-old bone, or a beautiful accident.

spotlights.name: YBC 7289: the square root of 2 on clay
spotlights.spot_it: A small round clay tablet, the size of a palm, scratched with a square, its two diagonals and cuneiform numbers.
spotlights.story_md: A student in southern Mesopotamia drew a square with side 30 and wrote along the diagonal the number **1;24,51,10** in base 60. In decimals that is **1.41421296**. The true square root of 2 is 1.41421356. The error is less than one part in a million, the most accurate calculation known from the ancient world. Next to it the student wrote 42;25,35, the diagonal's length. This is a school exercise, a **hand tablet** that fitted in a palm. It shows Babylonians knew the diagonal-of-a-square rule more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. It is kept in the **Yale Babylonian Collection**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows serious computation, and the Pythagorean rule, 3,700 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A schoolkid's homework, accurate to six decimal places.

spotlights.name: Plimpton 322
spotlights.spot_it: A broken clay tablet with four columns and fifteen rows of cuneiform numbers, its left edge snapped off.
spotlights.story_md: Publisher **George Plimpton** bought this tablet from dealer **Edgar Banks** around 1922 and left it to **Columbia University**. It probably comes from **Larsa** in southern Iraq. Each of its **15 rows** relates to a **Pythagorean triple**, whole numbers such as 119, 169 and 120 that form a right-angled triangle. Some triples are large: 12,709 and 18,541 in one row. Nobody finds those by trial and error, so the scribe had a method. What the table was for is still argued: a teacher's answer key, a list of reciprocals, or, in one disputed 2017 claim, an early trigonometric table.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows systematic number theory in the Old Babylonian period.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifteen right triangles, a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.

spotlights.name: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus
spotlights.spot_it: A long papyrus scroll in red and black hieratic script, packed with tables and small worked problems.
spotlights.story_md: The scribe **Ahmes** copied it around **1550 BCE** from an older text, and it is one of the best sources we have on Egyptian mathematics. It opens by promising insight into all that exists. Inside are **84 problems**: dividing loaves among men, the volume of granaries, the slope of a pyramid, and a table for writing fractions such as 2/n as sums of unit fractions, since Egyptians wrote nearly all fractions that way. One problem estimates the area of a circle, which works out to a value of pi of about **3.16**. Scottish lawyer **Henry Rhind** bought it in Luxor in **1858**; it is now in the British Museum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a window into how maths was taught, as recipes for real tasks.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ahmes, the first mathematician whose name we know, was a copyist.

spotlights.name: Quipu, the Inca knot record
spotlights.spot_it: A main cord with dozens of coloured strings hanging from it, each tied with clusters of knots at different heights.
spotlights.story_md: The Inca ran an empire of perhaps 10 million people along the Andes with no written script. Accounts were kept on **quipus** (khipu): cords knotted in a **base-10 place system**. Knot type and position give the digits: clusters near the top are hundreds or thousands, lower clusters tens, and the lowest knots units. An empty space works as zero. Trained keepers, the *quipucamayoc*, read them for taxes, census and stores. Spanish chroniclers saw them used to settle disputes. About **1,000** survive. Some may also encode narrative, which nobody has yet cracked.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows place value invented independently, in string.
spotlights.memory_hook: An empire's spreadsheet, tied in knots.

sections.title: The Greek bet: prove it
sections.intro_md:
Babylonians and Egyptians knew many true rules. What they did not leave behind is **proof**. Greek thinkers from about **600 BCE** made a different bet: do not just say the rule works, show why it must work, starting from statements nobody can deny.

The idea reached its peak in **Euclid's Elements**, written in Alexandria around **300 BCE**. Euclid starts with **5 postulates** and **5 common notions** and builds **465 propositions**, each proved only from what came before. Generations learned to reason from it, and it remained a school textbook into the 20th century.

The Greeks also hit the first crisis. If the side of a square is 1, its diagonal is the square root of 2, and a short proof shows that number **cannot be written as a fraction**. Lengths existed that whole numbers could not express. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned the man who revealed it. The legend is late and doubtful. The shock was real.

spotlights.name: Pythagoras and the irrational shock
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded marble head in a headband, a Roman copy; the face is a guess, since no portrait from life survives.
spotlights.story_md: **Pythagoras** ran a community on Croton in southern Italy that mixed mathematics, music and strict rules, including a ban on eating beans. He left no writings, and almost everything about him was written centuries later. The theorem with his name was known long before: Babylonian tablets and India's Shulba Sutras use it. What his followers did push was the idea that **all things are number**, backed by a real discovery: strings whose lengths are in simple ratios like 2:1 and 3:2 sound harmonious. Then came the proof that the square root of 2 is **irrational**. The story that **Hippasus** was drowned for revealing it appears only in late sources.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His school made number the key to nature, the hope behind all mathematical physics.
spotlights.memory_hook: All is number, until the diagonal of a square refused to be one.

spotlights.name: Euclid's Elements
spotlights.spot_it: A brown papyrus scrap with Greek letters and a little diagram, or a Venetian printed page with geometric figures in the margin.
spotlights.story_md: Euclid is a name with almost no biography, but his book is a monument. Its **13 books** cover plane geometry, ratios, number theory and the five Platonic solids. Book IX contains a proof that **there is no largest prime**: multiply any finite list of primes, add 1, and the result has a prime factor not on the list. The oldest papyrus with its text, found at **Oxyrhynchus** in Egypt, is a schoolchild's scrap of Book II. **Erhard Ratdolt** printed it in Venice in **1482**. It is often estimated to have had more editions than any book except the Bible.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the model every later mathematics followed: definitions, axioms, proofs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirteen books, 465 proofs, 2,300 years in print.

spotlights.name: The Archimedes Palimpsest
spotlights.spot_it: A stained parchment page with a prayer book's text written over faint, sideways Greek lines and diagrams.
spotlights.story_md: In about **950** a scribe in Constantinople copied works of **Archimedes**. On **13 April 1229** monks scraped and washed the parchment and wrote a prayer book over it. In **1906** Danish scholar **Johan Heiberg** spotted the ghost text in Istanbul. The book then vanished, suffered mould in a French cellar, gained forged gold paintings, and sold at Christie's in **1998 for $2 million**. Imaging at the Walters Art Museum recovered the hidden text, including the only copy of **The Method**, where Archimedes explains how he found volumes by imagining weighing slices on a balance, an approach close to integral calculus, 1,900 years before Newton.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how near the ancient world came to calculus, and how close we came to losing it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Archimedes' calculus, hidden under a prayer book for 700 years.

sections.title: India: altars, zero and the place-value machine
sections.intro_md:
The numerals you use every day, 0 to 9 with place value, were made in **India**. Arab scholars called them Indian numbers; Europe later called them Arabic. The idea is simple and enormous: ten symbols, where position sets value, and a symbol for **nothing** that holds a place.

The road there is long. The **Shulba Sutras**, manuals for building Vedic fire altars from perhaps **800 to 500 BCE**, state the diagonal rule and approximate the square root of 2. The prosody scholar **Pingala** counted poetic metres with patterns that amount to binary numbers. **Aryabhata** in **499 CE** used place value to compute and gave pi as about 3.1416.

In **628 CE**, **Brahmagupta** did something new: he treated **zero as a number** with its own rules of arithmetic, alongside negative numbers he called debts. The oldest firmly dated Indian zero symbol in stone, a small circle, is carved in a temple at **Gwalior** in **876 CE**.

spotlights.name: The Shulba Sutras
spotlights.spot_it: Ritual instructions in Sanskrit for laying bricks into altars shaped like a falcon, a tortoise or a wheel.
spotlights.story_md: Vedic ritual demanded fire altars of exact shapes and areas, built with cords and pegs. The **Shulba Sutras** (*shulba* means cord) give the geometry. **Baudhayana** states that the diagonal of a rectangle produces both areas its sides produce separately: the Pythagorean rule, with examples like 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13. He gives the square root of 2 as 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3x4) minus 1/(3x4x34), which is **577/408**, correct to five decimal places. There are rules to turn a square into a circle of nearly the same area. A man who desires heaven, one text says, should build an altar in the form of a **falcon**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's oldest surviving geometry, written for building, not for proof.
spotlights.memory_hook: A falcon-shaped altar that needed the square root of 2.

spotlights.name: Pingala's metres and the binary code
spotlights.spot_it: Sanskrit verse patterns of short and long syllables listed in a fixed order, like 0s and 1s.
spotlights.story_md: **Pingala** wrote the *Chandaḥśāstra*, a treatise on Sanskrit metre. Each line is a pattern of **light (laghu)** and **heavy (guru)** syllables. To list all possible patterns, Pingala gave rules that work exactly like counting in **binary**, with light and heavy in place of 0 and 1. Later commentators, notably **Halayudha** in the 10th century, drew the table of combinations that Europe knows as **Pascal's triangle**, calling it *meru prastara*, the staircase of Mount Meru. Counting the metres of a given length leads to the numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, known in Europe as **Fibonacci numbers**, discussed by Virahanka and Hemachandra before Fibonacci.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Poetry, not commerce, pushed Indian scholars into combinatorics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Short and long syllables: binary, two thousand years early.

spotlights.name: Aryabhata
spotlights.spot_it: A seated statue in the gardens of IUCAA in Pune, or India's first satellite, a 26-sided drum launched in 1975 and named after him.
spotlights.story_md: At 23, **Aryabhata** wrote the *Aryabhatiya*, 121 verses on astronomy and mathematics. He used a place-value system, gave **pi as 62,832/20,000 = 3.1416**, and called the value approximate, which some read as a hint that pi is irrational. He built a table of sines, and proposed that the **Earth rotates** on its axis, explaining the daily turning of the stars, an idea most later Indian astronomers rejected. He also explained eclipses by shadows, not by the demon Rahu. India's first satellite, launched from the Soviet Union on **19 April 1975**, carried his name, and appeared on the 2-rupee note.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the first great named figure of classical Indian mathematics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pi to four places and a spinning Earth, at 23.

spotlights.name: The Bakhshali manuscript
spotlights.spot_it: Fragile birch-bark leaves in Sharada script, with small black dots used as zero in place-value numbers.
spotlights.story_md: A farmer dug up **70 leaves of birch bark** near the village of **Bakhshali**, close to Mardan in today's Pakistan, in **1881**. The text is an arithmetic handbook with problems on profit, travel and equations, and it uses a **dot as a placeholder zero**, the *shunya-bindu*. In **2017** the Bodleian Library announced carbon dates: one leaf from **224 to 383 CE**, which would make it the oldest written zero. Scholars objected, because other leaves dated centuries later and the claim came by press release. In **2024** Oxford revised the dating to about **799 to 1102 CE**. The dot is real; how old it is remains open.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a key witness to zero, and a lesson in how dates get contested.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dot on birch bark that started a dating fight.

spotlights.name: The Gwalior zero and Brahmagupta's rules
spotlights.spot_it: A small rock-cut Vishnu shrine on Gwalior Fort; inside, an inscription where 270 is written with a little round 0.
spotlights.story_md: In **628 CE**, in the *Brahmasphutasiddhanta*, **Brahmagupta** wrote rules for zero as a number: a number minus itself is zero, zero added to a number leaves it unchanged, zero times anything is zero. He handled negative numbers as **debts** and positives as **fortunes**. He also said zero divided by zero is zero, which mathematics later rejected. Two and a half centuries later, a donor's inscription in the **Chaturbhuj temple** at Gwalior Fort recorded a garden **270 hastas** long and gifts of **50 garlands** a day, using a circle for zero. Dated **876 CE**, it is one of the oldest Indian zeros in stone.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Zero as a number, not just a gap, is India's most famous gift to mathematics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Debts, fortunes and nothing: the three new numbers of 628.

sections.title: India: infinite series, Ramanujan and the moderns
sections.intro_md:
Indian mathematics did not stop with zero. In **Kerala**, between the **14th and 16th centuries**, a line of teachers and students founded by **Madhava of Sangamagrama** found infinite series for pi, sine and cosine that Europe found again only with Gregory, Newton and Leibniz in the 1600s. Whether any of this reached Europe through Jesuit missionaries is a debated idea with **no direct evidence**.

Then came the most romantic story in modern mathematics. A clerk in **Madras** with almost no formal training mailed nine pages of formulas to a Cambridge professor in **1913**, and became a Fellow of the Royal Society five years later. Since **2012**, India marks his birthday, **22 December**, as **National Mathematics Day**.

India's mathematical culture runs wide: a schoolteacher in Devlali who found a strange number, a woman who multiplied 13-digit numbers in her head, and the Indian Statistical Institute that shaped how India counts itself. Indian-born or Indian-origin mathematicians have won Fields Medals: **Manjul Bhargava** in 2014 and **Akshay Venkatesh** in 2018.

spotlights.name: Madhava and the Kerala school
spotlights.spot_it: Malayalam and Sanskrit palm-leaf texts with verses that, in modern notation, read as infinite sums.
spotlights.story_md: **Madhava** lived in Sangamagrama near today's Irinjalakuda in Kerala. None of his mathematical writing survives directly; his results are known through students such as **Nilakantha Somayaji** and **Jyeshthadeva**, whose *Yuktibhasa* (about **1530**, in Malayalam) gives proofs. The results include **pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ...**, now called the **Madhava-Leibniz series**, and the power series for sine and cosine. Because that series converges slowly, Madhava added correction terms and got pi correct to **11 decimal places**. Europe reached these series about 250 years later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is calculus-style thinking in India two centuries before Newton.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pi as an endless sum, in Kerala, before Columbus sailed.

spotlights.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
spotlights.spot_it: A passport-style photo of a young man with a round face and wavy hair; his childhood home is a tiled house on Sarangapani Street, Kumbakonam.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Erode** and raised in **Kumbakonam**, Ramanujan failed college exams because he studied only mathematics. On **16 January 1913**, as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust, he sent **G. H. Hardy** nine pages of results. Hardy first suspected fraud, then decided they had to be true because no one could invent them. Ramanujan reached Cambridge in 1914 and was elected **FRS in 1918**. He left nearly **3,900 results**. Visiting him ill in hospital, Hardy said his taxi, **1729**, was a dull number. Ramanujan replied it is the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two ways: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed, and 9 cubed plus 10 cubed. He died at **32**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His formulas are still being proved and used, in fields from string theory to computing pi.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1729: the taxi number that was not dull.

spotlights.name: Kaprekar's constant, 6174
spotlights.spot_it: Take a four-digit number, sort its digits high-to-low and low-to-high, subtract, repeat: you always land on 6174.
spotlights.story_md: **D. R. Kaprekar** taught at a government junior school in **Devlali**, Maharashtra, from 1930 to 1962, and played with numbers in his spare time. He found this routine: pick any four-digit number whose digits are not all the same, say 3524. Arrange its digits in descending and ascending order and subtract: 5432 minus 2345 is 3087. Repeat: 8730 minus 0378 is 8352, then 8532 minus 2358 is **6174**, and 7641 minus 1467 gives 6174 forever. Every such number gets there in **at most seven steps**. Indian journals ignored him for years; Martin Gardner's **1975** column in *Scientific American* made him known worldwide.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how much a curious amateur can find with simple tools.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every four-digit road leads to 6174.

spotlights.name: Shakuntala Devi, the human computer
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling woman in a sari beside a blackboard of huge numbers; the 2020 film starring Vidya Balan told her story.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Bangalore**, Shakuntala Devi toured with arithmetic shows from childhood. On **18 June 1980**, at **Imperial College London**, the computing department picked two random 13-digit numbers: 7,686,369,774,870 times 2,465,099,745,779. She gave the 26-digit answer in **28 seconds**. The feat entered the **1982 Guinness Book of Records**. In **1988** psychologist **Arthur Jensen** at Berkeley tested her: she gave the cube root of 61,629,875 (it is 395) before he finished writing the problem down. Mental calculation is a different skill from mathematics, but her shows made millions of Indians curious about numbers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made numbers a public spectacle in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-six digits in twenty-eight seconds.

sections.title: From Baghdad to Pisa
sections.intro_md:
Indian numerals travelled west through the **Islamic world**. In the **House of Wisdom** in Baghdad, under the Abbasid caliphs, scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works and built on them. Around **825**, **al-Khwarizmi** wrote a book on calculating with Hindu numerals; its Latin version began *Algoritmi dicit*, "so says al-Khwarizmi", which gave us the word **algorithm**. His other book gave us **algebra**, from *al-jabr*, restoring.

Europe was slow. Roman numerals were hard to calculate with, so merchants used counting boards. In **1202** **Leonardo of Pisa**, later called **Fibonacci**, who had learned Hindu-Arabic numerals as a boy in North Africa, published *Liber Abaci* to teach them to merchants. Some cities resisted: a **1299** Florence rule told bankers to write amounts in words or Roman numerals, because Arabic digits were easy to forge.

The Islamic world also built mathematics into its buildings, in geometric tile patterns that modern physics only learned to describe in the 1980s.

spotlights.name: Al-Khwarizmi
spotlights.spot_it: A Soviet 1983 stamp shows a bearded scholar in a turban; no portrait from life exists.
spotlights.story_md: **Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi** worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad. His book *al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala* (about **820**) taught how to solve linear and quadratic equations, with no symbols at all, entirely in words, and with geometric proofs. *Al-jabr*, restoring, moved a subtracted term to the other side of an equation; it became **algebra**. His book on Indian numerals survives only in Latin, opening with **Algoritmi dicit**. His name became **algorithm**, the word at the heart of every computer program. The Spanish *guarismo*, digit, also comes from his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two of the most used words in modern science come from one man.
spotlights.memory_hook: Algebra and algorithm: one scholar, two words.

spotlights.name: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
spotlights.spot_it: A medieval manuscript page with Hindu-Arabic numerals in a boxed column on the margin.
spotlights.story_md: **Leonardo of Pisa** grew up partly in **Bugia** (Béjaïa, Algeria), where his father ran a Pisan trading post, and learned Indian numerals there. *Liber Abaci* opens by naming the nine Indian figures and the sign 0, with which any number may be written. Most of the book is practical: currency conversion, profit sharing, interest. One puzzle asks how many pairs of rabbits there will be after a year if each pair produces a new pair monthly from its second month. The answer gives **1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...**, now called the **Fibonacci sequence**, a name only attached in the 19th century, and already described in India by Virahanka and Hemachandra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Europe switched to the numerals the whole world now uses.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rabbit puzzle, an Indian sequence, an Italian name.

spotlights.name: Girih tiles at Darb-i Imam
spotlights.spot_it: Interlaced star-and-polygon strapwork in blue, white and gold on the walls of a Persian shrine, never quite repeating.
spotlights.story_md: Islamic artists from about **1200** made patterns using a set of **five tile shapes** whose angles are all multiples of **36 degrees**. In **2007** physicists **Peter Lu** and **Paul Steinhardt** showed in *Science* that the patterns on the **Darb-i Imam shrine** in Isfahan, built in **1453**, come close to **quasicrystalline** order: they never repeat, yet follow strict rules, like Roger Penrose's tilings of the **1970s**. Quasicrystals were found in real metal by Dan Shechtman in **1982**, a discovery so disbelieved it won a Nobel only in **2011**. The craftsmen probably used the tiles as a design tool, not a theory, which is part of the wonder.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Art reached a mathematical structure centuries before mathematics named it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pattern that never repeats, on a wall from 1453.

sections.title: How a proof actually works
sections.intro_md:
A proof is not an experiment. You cannot prove that every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes by checking a few trillion of them; people have, and it is still unproved (that is the **Goldbach conjecture**, 1742). A proof must cover **every case at once**.

Mathematicians use a small toolkit. **Direct proof** chains facts forward. **Proof by contradiction** assumes the opposite and shows it leads to nonsense, the way the square root of 2 is shown to be irrational. **Induction** proves a statement for 1, then shows that if it holds for any number it holds for the next, like knocking down an endless row of dominoes. **Construction** builds the object you claim exists.

Everything rests on **axioms**, and changing an axiom can create a new mathematics. That is what happened when people finally doubted Euclid's fifth postulate. Proofs also changed in another way: some are now too long for any human to check alone, and are checked by computers.

spotlights.name: Euclid's fifth postulate and the new geometries
spotlights.spot_it: Triangles drawn on a saddle or a sphere whose angles do not add up to 180 degrees.
spotlights.story_md: Euclid's **fifth postulate** says, in modern form, that through a point off a line exactly one parallel line can be drawn. It looked less obvious than the others, and for 2,000 years people tried to prove it from them. In **1829** **Nikolai Lobachevsky** in Kazan, and in **1832** **János Bolyai** in Hungary, gave up and built a **consistent geometry where it is false**. Gauss had privately reached the same idea and kept quiet. In **1854** **Bernhard Riemann** generalised geometry to curved spaces of any dimension. Sixty years later, Einstein needed exactly that to describe gravity as curved spacetime.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved axioms are choices, and a pure choice later described the universe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Change one axiom and you get the geometry of gravity.

spotlights.name: The seven bridges of Königsberg
spotlights.spot_it: An old city map with an island, a river splitting in two and seven bridges linking four land areas.
spotlights.story_md: The people of Königsberg in Prussia (today **Kaliningrad**, Russia) asked whether you could walk through the city crossing each of its **seven bridges exactly once**. In **1736** **Leonhard Euler** showed it was impossible, and the reason was new. Distances and shapes did not matter, only which land areas connect to which. Each area touched an odd number of bridges, and a walk that uses every bridge once allows at most two such areas, the start and the end. That insight founded **graph theory** and **topology**. Graph theory now runs route planners, social networks and the internet's routing. Two of the bridges were destroyed in WWII.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows abstraction at work: throw away the details and the answer appears.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven bridges, one walk, no way to do it.

spotlights.name: The four colour theorem
spotlights.spot_it: A map coloured with only four colours where no two neighbouring regions share one.
spotlights.story_md: In **1852** **Francis Guthrie**, colouring the counties of England, noticed that four colours always seemed enough so that no neighbours match. For 124 years nobody could prove it. In **1976** **Kenneth Appel** and **Wolfgang Haken** at Illinois reduced it to **1,834 configurations** (later 1,482) and had a computer check them, which took **over a thousand hours** of machine time. Many mathematicians refused to call it a proof, since no human could check it. Errors were found and fixed by 1989. In **2005** **Georges Gonthier** checked the whole proof in the **Coq** proof assistant. It is now accepted, and it opened the door to machine proof.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It forced mathematics to ask whether a proof must be readable by a person.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four colours, a thousand computer hours, one argument about what proof means.

sections.title: Infinity breaks, logic patches it, almost
sections.intro_md:
By 1900 mathematics looked unstoppable, and mathematicians wanted to put it on a perfectly safe base. Instead they found cracks.

**Georg Cantor** showed infinities come in **different sizes**, which many contemporaries found offensive. **Bertrand Russell** found a paradox in the simplest idea of a set. The response was to rebuild mathematics from pure logic, and **David Hilbert** in the 1920s set out a programme: write all of mathematics as a formal system, then prove that system **complete** (every true statement provable) and **consistent** (no contradictions).

In **1931** a 25-year-old Austrian, **Kurt Gödel**, showed that cannot be done. Any consistent system strong enough for basic arithmetic contains **true statements it cannot prove**, and cannot prove its own consistency. In **1936** **Alan Turing** showed that no mechanical procedure can decide every mathematical question, and in the process described the computer.

Mathematics survived, and works as well as ever. But it lost the dream of total certainty, and gained the idea of computation.

spotlights.name: Cantor's infinities
spotlights.spot_it: A list of decimals with a diagonal line through it, each digit changed, producing a number that is on no line of the list.
spotlights.story_md: **Georg Cantor** in Halle asked whether all infinities are equal. The whole numbers and the fractions turn out to be the **same size**: you can pair them off one to one. But in **1891** his **diagonal argument** showed the real numbers are **bigger**. Take any claimed list of all decimals between 0 and 1, change the first digit of the first, the second digit of the second, and so on: the new number differs from every entry. So there are more points on a line than whole numbers, infinitely more. Leopold Kronecker attacked his work; Hilbert later said no one shall expel us from the paradise Cantor created.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made infinity a precise object, and set up the crisis of the next 40 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Some infinities are bigger than others.

spotlights.name: Russell's paradox and Principia Mathematica
spotlights.spot_it: A thick three-volume book of dense logical symbols where 1 + 1 = 2 is only established hundreds of pages in.
spotlights.story_md: In **1901** **Bertrand Russell** considered the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? If yes, then no; if no, then yes. In **1902** he wrote to **Gottlob Frege**, whose logic book was in press, and Frege saw his life's work shaken. Russell and **Alfred North Whitehead** then tried to rebuild mathematics on safe logic in *Principia Mathematica*. In the first edition, the proposition from which 1 + 1 = 2 will follow arrives on **page 379** of Volume I; the proof is completed in Volume II, with the dry note that the proposition is **occasionally useful**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how much hidden machinery sits under the simplest arithmetic.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three hundred and seventy-nine pages to reach one plus one.

spotlights.name: Kurt Gödel and incompleteness
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man in round glasses and a dark suit, often photographed walking beside Einstein in Princeton.
spotlights.story_md: **Kurt Gödel** built a statement that says, in effect, **this statement cannot be proved** in the system. If the system is consistent, the statement is true and unprovable. He did it by coding formulas as numbers, so arithmetic could talk about itself. Published in **1931**, when he was **25**, it ended Hilbert's dream. At the Institute for Advanced Study, Einstein said he went to his office mainly for the privilege of **walking home with Gödel**. At his US citizenship hearing in **1947** Gödel tried to explain a flaw he had found in the Constitution. Afraid of being poisoned, he starved to death in **1978**, weighing 29 kg.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous limit on what proof can ever do.
spotlights.memory_hook: This sentence cannot be proved, and it is true.

spotlights.name: Alan Turing and the limits of computation
spotlights.spot_it: A dark-haired man in a 1951 portrait; his imagined machine is a head reading and writing symbols on an endless tape.
spotlights.story_md: Hilbert also asked for a mechanical method to decide any mathematical statement, the *Entscheidungsproblem*. In **1936**, at **24**, **Alan Turing** answered no. To do it he defined what a mechanical method is: an imaginary **machine** with a tape, a head and a table of rules. He showed one universal machine can imitate any other, which is the idea of the **stored-program computer**. Then he proved no machine can decide, for every program, whether it will ever **halt**. In the war he helped break German **Enigma** codes at Bletchley Park. He was prosecuted for homosexuality in **1952** and died in 1954; the UK pardoned him posthumously in 2013.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The computer was invented as a by-product of a question about proof.
spotlights.memory_hook: To prove machines have limits, he first had to invent the machine.

sections.title: So why does it work? The best answers
sections.intro_md:
Back to Wigner's question. Philosophers and mathematicians give four main answers, and most people mix them.

**Platonism** says mathematical objects really exist, outside space and time, and we **discover** them. Many working mathematicians feel this way: the primes seem to be there before anyone looks. **Formalism** says mathematics is a game of symbols played by rules, and its truth is just provability. **Intuitionism**, from L. E. J. Brouwer, says mathematics is a human mental construction, and only what can be built counts. **Structuralism** says mathematics is the science of pattern itself, and the world is full of patterns.

Practical explanations help too. Much mathematics **started from the world**: geometry from land, calculus from motion. Mathematicians produce a vast stock of structures, and physicists pick the few that fit, so we remember the hits. **Symmetry** does deep work: Emmy Noether proved that every continuous symmetry of a physical law gives a conservation law. And sometimes the fit is simply eerie, as when colliding blocks count out the digits of pi.

Nobody has closed the question. That is part of why it is fun.

spotlights.name: G. H. Hardy and the joy of useless maths
spotlights.spot_it: A slim Englishman in a 1920s photograph; the author of a thin, elegant book defending pure mathematics.
spotlights.story_md: **Godfrey Harold Hardy** was the leading English pure mathematician of his day and Ramanujan's champion. In *A Mathematician's Apology* (**1940**) he argued that real mathematics is justified by **beauty**, like poetry, and boasted that number theory and relativity had no use in war. He was wrong twice: relativity led to the bomb and to GPS, and number theory now guards every online payment through **RSA** encryption. Hardy also said his greatest contribution to mathematics was discovering Ramanujan. Paul Erdős later recalled that Hardy rated mathematicians on a scale of 0 to 100: himself 25, Hilbert 80, Ramanujan **100**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the best example of pure mathematics becoming useful against its maker's wishes.
spotlights.memory_hook: He bragged his maths was useless; now it protects your bank card.

spotlights.name: David Hilbert
spotlights.spot_it: A man with a pointed beard, round glasses and a Panama hat in a 1912 postcard portrait.
spotlights.story_md: At the **1900** International Congress in Paris, **David Hilbert** listed **23 problems** for the new century, a list that shaped mathematics for a hundred years. He led Göttingen, the world centre of mathematics, and championed **formalism**: put mathematics on axioms and prove they never contradict each other. His motto, spoken in **1930**, was **we must know, we will know**, and it is carved on his gravestone. The day before he said it, Gödel announced the first incompleteness theorem at a meeting in the same city, Königsberg. Hilbert also defended Emmy Noether's right to teach when colleagues objected to a woman.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shaped the agenda and the self-image of 20th-century mathematics.
spotlights.memory_hook: We must know, we will know: said one day after Gödel showed we cannot.

spotlights.name: Emmy Noether and symmetry
spotlights.spot_it: A round-faced woman with glasses and her hair pulled back, in a portrait from around 1900.
spotlights.story_md: In **1915** Hilbert and Felix Klein invited **Emmy Noether** to Göttingen to help with Einstein's new theory. Faculty members objected to a woman lecturing, so for years her courses were advertised under **Hilbert's name** and she was unpaid. She proved what is now **Noether's theorem**: every continuous symmetry of a physical law matches a conserved quantity. Laws that do not change over time give **conservation of energy**; laws that do not change from place to place give conservation of momentum. She then helped found **modern abstract algebra**. Expelled by the Nazis in **1933**, she moved to Bryn Mawr College and died there in **1935**, aged 53.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the deepest reasons mathematics fits physics: symmetry is mathematical.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same law tomorrow means energy is conserved.

spotlights.name: The blocks that count pi
spotlights.spot_it: An animation of a big block sliding into a small one by a wall, with a counter of collisions that spells 3, 31, 314, 3141.
spotlights.story_md: Put a small block between a wall and a big block, and push the big one toward it. Count every collision, block with block and block with wall, with no friction and perfectly elastic bounces. If the big block is **100 times** heavier, there are **31** collisions. If it is **10,000 times** heavier, **314**. At a million times, **3,141**. The count spells out the **digits of pi**. Mathematician **Gregory Galperin** published this in **2003**. The reason is that conservation of energy draws a circle in the right coordinates, and each collision steps around it by a tiny angle. Pi hides wherever there is a circle, even when no circle is visible.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a small, testable case of Wigner's mystery, with an explanation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bang, bang, bang: 3.14159.

sections.title: Useless, until it wasn't
sections.intro_md:
The strongest evidence for Wigner's puzzle is the **time lag**. Again and again, ideas developed for their own sake waited decades or centuries for a use nobody could foresee.

The Greek study of **conic sections**, about 200 BCE, waited 1,800 years until Kepler found that planets move in ellipses. **Boolean algebra** (1854) waited until Claude Shannon in **1937** saw it could design switching circuits, the logic of every chip. **Riemann's** curved geometry of 1854 became Einstein's gravity in 1915, and today **GPS** would drift by kilometres a day without it.

The pattern is not proof of anything mystical. Mathematicians explore every structure they can, so some of them were bound to fit later. But the hit rate is striking, and it is a practical argument for funding pure research. The bar chart shows the gap between the idea and the use.

spotlights.name: GPS and Einstein's corrections
spotlights.spot_it: A boxy satellite with two long solar-panel wings, one of about 30 orbiting 20,000 km up.
spotlights.story_md: GPS works by timing signals from satellites, so its clocks must agree to billionths of a second. Two effects from relativity fight. The satellites move fast, so by **special relativity** their clocks run slow by about **7 microseconds a day**. They sit higher in Earth's gravity, so by **general relativity** they run fast by about **46 microseconds a day**. Net: **38 microseconds a day** fast. Uncorrected, positions would drift by about **11 km a day**. So engineers set each satellite clock slightly slow before launch: **10.22999999543 MHz** instead of 10.23 MHz. Riemann's geometry is inside your phone's map.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the everyday proof that pure geometry runs the modern world.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty-eight microseconds a day, or you miss by 11 km.

spotlights.name: RSA: prime numbers guard the internet
spotlights.when: Published 1977; GCHQ found it secretly in 1973
spotlights.spot_it: Three men in a 2003 photo, Shamir, Rivest and Adleman, whose initials name the code.
spotlights.story_md: Multiplying two large primes is easy. Splitting the product back into them is, as far as anyone knows, **extremely hard** for ordinary computers. In **1977** **Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman** at MIT turned that into **public-key encryption**: you publish the product as a lock anyone can close, and only you, knowing the primes, can open it. The maths underneath is **Fermat's little theorem** of **1640** and Euler's work of the 1700s, pure number theory. The British spy agency GCHQ's **Clifford Cocks** had found the same idea in **1973**, but it stayed secret until **1997**. Quantum computers could one day break it, so new codes are being rolled out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned Hardy's useless number theory into the lock on online money.
spotlights.memory_hook: Easy to multiply, hard to split: the internet's padlock.

spotlights.name: CT scanners and the Radon transform
spotlights.spot_it: A doughnut-shaped hospital scanner with a sliding bed; the image is a slice through the body built from X-rays taken around it.
spotlights.story_md: In **1917** Austrian mathematician **Johann Radon** solved a pure problem: if you know the integrals of a function along every straight line, can you recover the function? Yes, with an explicit formula. No one needed it for decades. In the **1960s** physicist **Allan Cormack** in South Africa and the US worked out how to rebuild a body's inside from X-ray beams sent through it, not knowing about Radon's work. Engineer **Godfrey Hounsfield** at EMI built the first scanner; the first patient was scanned in London in **1971**. Cormack and Hounsfield shared the **1979** Nobel in medicine. Neither was a medical doctor.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every CT scan reconstructs your insides with a 1917 formula.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lines through a body, a formula from 1917, a picture of your brain.

spotlights.name: Fourier and the sound of everything
spotlights.spot_it: A painted portrait of a French scientist in a high collar; his idea appears as a wiggly line built from stacked waves.
spotlights.story_md: **Joseph Fourier**, who had joined Napoleon's expedition to Egypt, was studying how heat flows in solid metal. In **1807** he claimed that any reasonable curve, even one with corners, can be built by adding up **simple sine waves**. Leading mathematicians including Lagrange doubted it, and making it rigorous took most of the 19th century. His book appeared in **1822**. Today **Fourier analysis** is how MP3 files throw away sounds you cannot hear, how **JPEG** compresses photos, how MRI scanners make images and how your phone separates radio signals. Fourier was also among the first to describe what we now call the **greenhouse effect**, in the 1820s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One heat equation idea became the basis of digital sound and images.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every song on your phone is a pile of Fourier's waves.

sections.title: Mathematics around the world
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics was not invented once and passed along a single line. Many cultures built it, often independently, and each left a recognisable style.

**China** produced *The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, compiled by about the 1st century CE, with methods for solving systems of equations that match what schools now call Gaussian elimination, and with **negative numbers** shown as black rods beside red positive ones. The **Maya** had a full place-value system in base 20 with a shell sign for zero. **Japan**, closed to the world during the Edo period, developed its own tradition, *wasan*, and hung geometry puzzles in temples. And across Asia the **abacus** made arithmetic physical and very fast.

Seeing these side by side does something useful. It shows that mathematics is a human universal, and that the same truths, like the diagonal rule and place value, turn up wherever people look hard enough.

spotlights.name: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art
spotlights.when: Compiled by about 1st century CE; commentary 263 CE
spotlights.spot_it: A Chinese printed book page in columns of characters, with problems on fields, grain and taxes.
spotlights.story_md: Nine chapters, **246 problems**, each with an answer and a method: fields, grain exchange, fair taxes, construction, right triangles. Chapter 8, *fangcheng*, solves systems of linear equations by arranging numbers in a grid and eliminating, the method Europe credits to Gauss. Coefficients were laid out with **counting rods** on a board: red rods for positive numbers, black for negative, the earliest systematic use of negative numbers anywhere. In **263 CE** **Liu Hui** added a commentary with proofs and computed pi to about 3.1416 using a polygon of **3,072 sides**. The book was the core of Chinese mathematical education for over a thousand years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows algebra and negative numbers fully at work outside Greece and India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red rods for profit, black rods for debt.

spotlights.name: Maya numbers and the Dresden Codex
spotlights.when: Codex c. 11th to 12th century; zero in Long Count from 36 BCE
spotlights.spot_it: A bark-paper page painted with gods, glyphs and columns of dots, bars and shell signs.
spotlights.story_md: The Maya wrote numbers with three signs: a **dot for 1**, a **bar for 5** and a **shell for zero**, stacked vertically in **base 20**. Their calendar counted days from a fixed starting point, and the earliest known Long Count date using the zero placeholder, on Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo, is from **36 BCE**. The **Dresden Codex**, one of only **four** Maya books to survive Spanish burning, holds tables that predict **eclipses** and track Venus over decades. It reached Dresden in **1739** and was damaged by water during the bombing of the city in **1945**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a second, independent invention of place value with zero.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dot, bar, shell: zero in the jungle.

spotlights.name: Sangaku: geometry offered at temples
spotlights.spot_it: A painted wooden tablet hung under a shrine roof, with coloured circles packed inside triangles and a problem written beside them.
spotlights.story_md: During Japan's isolation, mathematicians of the *wasan* tradition, from samurai to farmers and children, painted geometry problems on wooden tablets and **hung them at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples**, as offerings and as public challenges. Typical problems ask for the radius of circles packed inside a triangle or a fan. About **900** tablets survive. Some problems are hard enough to need techniques that Western mathematicians developed separately. Some tablets give only the answer, daring visitors to find the proof. They are art, devotion and showing off at once.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows mathematics as a popular, even religious, pastime.
spotlights.memory_hook: A geometry problem, offered to the gods.

spotlights.name: The abacus (soroban)
spotlights.when: Japanese form from the 1600s; modern 1+4 bead form 1930s
spotlights.spot_it: A wooden frame with rods of beads: one bead above the bar and four below on each rod.
spotlights.story_md: The counting board is ancient; the **Chinese suanpan** spread across East Asia, and Japan's **soroban** slimmed it to **one bead worth 5 above the bar and four beads worth 1 below**. Each rod is a decimal place, so the abacus is place value you can touch. Trained users get so fast that they move to **anzan**: imagining the beads and calculating in their heads. In a famous **1946** contest in Tokyo, a soroban operator beat a US Army clerk with an electric calculator in four of five rounds. Abacus classes remain popular across Asia, and in India they are a common after-school activity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the place-value idea can live in the hand and then in the mind.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five above, ones below: a calculator made of wood.

sections.title: Where number comes from in the mind
sections.intro_md:
Is mathematics built into us? Partly. Babies, monkeys, fish, chicks and bees can tell **more from fewer** without counting. Psychologists call this the **approximate number system**. It is fuzzy, and works by ratio: telling 8 dots from 16 is easy, 15 from 16 is hard.

Exact number seems to need **language and culture**. The **Piraha** of the Amazon have words that work like "few" and "more" rather than "one" and "two". In experiments in 2008, they matched small quantities easily but made more errors with larger exact quantities, though they clearly grasp the idea of one. Children everywhere learn number words slowly, mastering "one", then "two", then "three", before the counting principle suddenly clicks, around age four.

This gives one answer to Wigner. Our minds may be shaped by evolution to model a world with objects, sizes and motion, so the maths we find natural is the maths that matches it. It does not explain why curved geometry or quantum matrices fit as well.

spotlights.name: Clever Hans, the horse who could not count
spotlights.spot_it: A white-gold horse in a Berlin courtyard, standing before a blackboard of numbers with an old man in a hat.
spotlights.story_md: **Wilhelm von Osten**, a Berlin maths teacher, taught his horse **Hans** to tap out answers with a hoof: sums, dates, even fractions. Crowds and a scientific commission were convinced. In **1907** psychologist **Oskar Pfungst** ran controlled tests. When Hans could see a questioner who knew the answer, he was right **89%** of the time. When he could not, he was right **6%**. Hans was reading tiny, unconscious changes in the questioner's posture as he approached the right number of taps. Von Osten was not a fraud; he fooled himself. The **Clever Hans effect** is why experiments today are run double-blind.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the classic warning: test whether the maths is in the animal or in you.
spotlights.memory_hook: The horse could read people, not numbers.

spotlights.name: Honeybees and nothing
spotlights.spot_it: A honeybee landing on a white card with a few black shapes, choosing the card with fewer.
spotlights.story_md: Researchers in **Australia and France** trained honeybees to choose the card with **fewer shapes**, rewarding them with sugar water. Then they showed a card with **no shapes at all**. The bees put the empty card at the low end of the scale, treating **nothing as less than one**, something children only manage around age four. The study by **Scarlett Howard** and colleagues appeared in *Science* in **2018**. Other work suggests bees keep a running count of landmarks up to about **four** while flying. A brain of under a million neurons can order quantities, which suggests number sense is cheap for evolution to build.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Number sense is old and widespread; it is not only a human invention.
spotlights.memory_hook: A brain smaller than a sesame seed rates zero below one.

sections.title: Five giants worth knowing
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics is often taught as if it had no people in it. It has many, and they are odd, brave and very different from each other.

Some were astonishingly productive: **Euler** wrote more mathematics than anyone before him, much of it after he went blind. Some were cautious perfectionists: **Gauss** sat on discoveries for decades, wanting them perfect. Some lived out of a suitcase: **Erdős** published with more than 500 collaborators. Some broke barriers: **Mirzakhani** became the first woman to win a Fields Medal. And some carry the field today, working in the open with blogs and machines: **Terence Tao**.

The Fields Medal, created in **1936** and given every four years to mathematicians **under 40**, is the field's best-known prize. Since there is no Nobel for mathematics, the **Abel Prize**, first given in **2003**, now plays that role for lifetime work.

spotlights.name: Leonhard Euler
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy-set man in a turban-like cap, painted in 1753 with one eye already failing.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Basel**, **Euler** worked in St Petersburg and Berlin and wrote around **850** works; his collected works run past **80 volumes**. He lost sight in one eye in his 30s and became almost totally blind by **1771**, then produced about half his work by dictation, doing huge calculations in his head. He gave us the notation **f(x)**, the letter **e**, **i** for the square root of minus one, and the sigma for sums, and made **pi** standard. His identity **e to the i pi plus 1 = 0** links the five most important constants in one line. Laplace told students: read Euler, he is the master of us all.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of the mathematical language you learned at school was set by him.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blind, dictating, and still out-writing everyone.

spotlights.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly man in a black velvet cap and dark coat, painted by Christian Albrecht Jensen in 1840.
spotlights.story_md: The son of a bricklayer in **Brunswick**, **Gauss** at 18 showed in **1796** that a regular **17-sided polygon** can be built with ruler and compass, the first advance on that question in 2,000 years. He reportedly asked for a 17-gon on his tombstone. At 24 he published *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*, the foundation of modern number theory. In **1801** he predicted where the lost dwarf planet **Ceres** would reappear, using a new method of least squares. He found non-Euclidean geometry privately but did not publish. His motto was **few, but ripe**. The famous story of him adding 1 to 100 as a schoolboy is told in many versions, and its details are shaky.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shaped number theory, statistics, geometry and physics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Few, but ripe: the perfectionist who sat on a revolution.

spotlights.name: Paul Erdős
spotlights.spot_it: A small, bald man in glasses, often in a rumpled suit, carrying everything he owned in one suitcase.
spotlights.story_md: **Paul Erdős** had no fixed home and no job for most of his life. He travelled from one mathematician to the next, arriving at the door to announce **my brain is open**, working for days, then moving on. He published about **1,500 papers** with more than **500 co-authors**, more than anyone in history. Mathematicians now measure their **Erdős number**: his co-authors have 1, their co-authors 2, and so on. He offered **cash prizes** for his open problems, from $25 to thousands of dollars. Hundreds of **Erdős problems** are listed online, and since **2025** they have become a test bed for AI.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed mathematics as a social, collaborative activity.
spotlights.memory_hook: My brain is open: 500 co-authors, one suitcase.

spotlights.name: Maryam Mirzakhani
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling woman with short hair, often photographed beside huge sheets of paper covered in curved doodles.
spotlights.story_md: Born in **Tehran**, **Mirzakhani** won gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad in **1994** and **1995**, the second time with a **perfect score**. At Harvard and then Stanford she studied the geometry of curved surfaces, such as how many simple closed loops of a given length lie on a hyperbolic surface. She worked by drawing on vast sheets laid on the floor; her young daughter thought her mother was painting. In **2014** she became the **first woman and the first Iranian** to win the Fields Medal. She died of breast cancer at **40**. Her birthday, **12 May**, is now **International Women in Mathematics Day**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She broke the Fields Medal's 78-year all-male run.
spotlights.memory_hook: Doodling on the floor all the way to a Fields Medal.

spotlights.name: Terence Tao
spotlights.spot_it: A cheerful man with glasses and a slight smile, an Australian-American at UCLA.
spotlights.story_md: **Terence Tao** was born in Adelaide to parents from Hong Kong. He won an IMO bronze at **10**, silver at 11 and gold at **12**, still the youngest gold medallist. He won the Fields Medal in **2006** for work across harmonic analysis, number theory and more; with Ben Green he proved that the primes contain **arithmetic progressions of any length**. He writes one of the most-read mathematics blogs and works openly on collaborative projects. Since 2023 he has been a leading voice on **AI in mathematics**, testing tools such as proof assistants and language models and also warning, in **2025**, against judging AI on results produced under unclear conditions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the living example of a mathematician who spans fields and tools.
spotlights.memory_hook: IMO gold at 12, and now refereeing the machines.

sections.title: The great problems
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics moves by **problems**. A good problem is easy to state, hard to solve and forces new ideas along the way.

Some of the most famous were posed as dares. **Fermat** scribbled one in a margin in **1637**. **Hilbert** listed 23 in **1900**. In **2000** the **Clay Mathematics Institute** named seven **Millennium Prize Problems** with **$1 million** each. Only one has been solved: the **Poincaré conjecture**, by a Russian who refused the money.

The most famous unsolved one is the **Riemann hypothesis**, from **1859**, which predicts how the primes are spread out. It has been checked for the first **10 trillion** zeros of the zeta function and nobody can prove it. Thousands of published results begin "assuming the Riemann hypothesis".

The table shows where the seven Millennium problems stand.

spotlights.name: Fermat's Last Theorem
spotlights.spot_it: A 17th-century French judge in a lace collar, and a modern Oxford professor at a blackboard: 358 years apart, one problem.
spotlights.story_md: **Pierre de Fermat**, a lawyer in Toulouse, wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus that **x^n + y^n = z^n** has no whole-number solutions when n is greater than 2, adding that he had a truly marvellous proof the margin was too narrow to contain. He almost certainly did not. **Andrew Wiles** read about it at **10** and later worked on it in secret for **seven years**. He announced a proof in Cambridge in **June 1993**; a gap was found in August. After nearly a year of despair, with **Richard Taylor**, he fixed it in **September 1994**. The proof appeared in **1995**. Wiles won the Abel Prize in **2016**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chasing it built much of modern number theory.
spotlights.memory_hook: A margin too small, and 358 years too long.

spotlights.name: Grigori Perelman and the Poincaré conjecture
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded man with dark, heavy eyebrows; one of very few photos, since he avoids the press.
spotlights.story_md: The **Poincaré conjecture** (1904) says, roughly, that any closed three-dimensional space with no holes is a sphere in disguise. In **November 2002** **Grigori Perelman** of St Petersburg posted the first of three papers online, not in a journal, that proved it by smoothing out space with **Ricci flow**, a method developed by **Richard Hamilton**. Experts spent years checking it. In **2006** he declined the Fields Medal, saying he was not interested in money or fame. In **2010** he refused the **$1 million** Millennium Prize, saying Hamilton's contribution was no less than his and that he disagreed with the organised mathematical community.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It solved one of the century's great problems and challenged how mathematics rewards people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Proved it, posted it, refused a million dollars.

spotlights.name: The Riemann hypothesis
spotlights.spot_it: A plot of a complex function with all its interesting zeros lined up exactly on one vertical line, the critical line.
spotlights.story_md: In an **eight-page paper** of **1859** on counting primes, **Bernhard Riemann** studied the **zeta function** and remarked that all its non-trivial zeros very probably lie on one line in the complex plane, and that he had put the question aside. If true, the primes are spread as evenly as they can be, and hundreds of theorems that assume it become unconditional. Computers have checked over **10 trillion** zeros: all on the line. That proves nothing, since mathematics is full of patterns that fail far out. It is on Hilbert's 1900 list and the Clay 2000 list, and is often called the most important open problem in mathematics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the deepest open question about the building blocks of arithmetic.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten trillion zeros on a line, still no proof.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics attracts legends, partly because it is hard to check them. Here are the most common, and what the evidence says.

**Einstein failed maths.** False. He had mastered calculus by about 15. When shown a 1935 claim that he had failed, he said he never failed in mathematics. **There is no Nobel in maths because a mathematician had an affair with Nobel's wife.** False: Nobel never married. He probably just did not think of mathematics as a practical field. **Pythagoras discovered Pythagoras' theorem.** Babylonian tablets and India's Shulba Sutras show it was known earlier; whether anyone proved it before the Greeks is unknown. **The golden ratio is everywhere.** Mostly myth, see below. **The young Gauss summed 1 to 100 in seconds.** The core of the story comes from a friend's memoir; the specific numbers were added later.

The real lesson is simple: check the source, and be suspicious of stories that are too neat.

spotlights.name: The golden ratio myth
spotlights.spot_it: A sliced nautilus shell with its chambers curling out, and the front of the Parthenon, the two most common 'golden ratio' pictures.
spotlights.story_md: The **golden ratio**, about **1.618**, is real and has lovely properties: it is the limit of ratios of Fibonacci numbers, and it appears in the regular pentagon. The myths are about where else it appears. The **nautilus shell** is a logarithmic spiral, but its growth ratio is usually closer to **1.33** than 1.618. Claims that the **Parthenon** was designed on it depend on where you choose to measure, and there is no ancient evidence the builders used it. Studies of whether people prefer golden rectangles give mixed results. Sunflower seed heads do show Fibonacci numbers, for good botanical reasons.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It teaches how easily a real number becomes a fake law.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1.618 is real; the nautilus did not get the memo.

spotlights.name: Did Einstein fail maths?
spotlights.spot_it: A 1921 photo of Albert Einstein with tidier hair than in the famous later shots.
spotlights.story_md: The story says even Einstein flunked mathematics, to comfort struggling students. In fact Einstein taught himself **Euclidean geometry** at about **12** and had mastered **differential and integral calculus** by about 15. He did fail the general entrance exam to the Zurich Polytechnic in **1895**, at 16, two years younger than usual, because of the non-science parts; his maths and physics marks were excellent. When a rabbi showed him a 1935 *Ripley's Believe It or Not* item claiming he had failed maths, he replied that he had never failed in mathematics. He did lean heavily on mathematician friends such as **Marcel Grossmann** for the geometry of general relativity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The truth is more useful than the myth: even Einstein needed help with Riemann's geometry.
spotlights.memory_hook: He never failed maths; he borrowed it from a friend.

sections.title: What is happening now: 2024 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
Mathematics changed faster in the last two years than in decades, mostly because of machines.

In **July 2025**, at the International Mathematical Olympiad on Australia's Sunshine Coast, an advanced version of **Google DeepMind's Gemini** scored **35 out of 42**, a gold-medal score, solving five of six problems in natural language within the time limit, graded by IMO coordinators. OpenAI claimed the same level; critics including Terence Tao said such claims needed controlled, reproducible conditions.

By 2026 the change reached research. In **May 2026** an OpenAI model produced a **counterexample to Erdős's 1946 unit distance conjecture**, verified and condensed by nine leading mathematicians on arXiv on **20 May**. In **September 2026** Anthropic released a complete **Lean 4** formal proof of **Fermat's Last Theorem**, about **13 million lines** written largely autonomously by Claude over 11 days; Kevin Buzzard checked it compiles. Humans are not out of a job: the **2026 Fields Medals** went to four people for deep human work, including **Hong Wang**, who with Joshua Zahl solved the three-dimensional **Kakeya conjecture** in 2025.

spotlights.name: Machines at the Maths Olympiad
spotlights.spot_it: Teenagers in rows of desks in a big hall, writing by hand for two 4.5-hour papers; in 2025, two AI labs entered unofficially.
spotlights.story_md: The **IMO** began in **Romania in 1959** with seven countries; now over 100 send six students each. In **2024** DeepMind's **AlphaProof** reached silver-medal level but needed problems translated into the **Lean** language and took days. In **July 2025**, an advanced **Gemini Deep Think** solved **five of six** problems in plain English within the **4.5-hour** limit and scored **35/42**, certified by IMO coordinators as gold standard. OpenAI announced a similar score for an experimental model, graded by former medallists. Human gold medallists still did better: several students scored a perfect 42.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marked the point where AI could write competition-level proofs in ordinary language.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five out of six, in 4.5 hours, in plain English.

spotlights.name: An AI counterexample to an Erdős conjecture
spotlights.spot_it: An arXiv paper whose nine authors include Fields medallists, titled as remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture.
spotlights.story_md: In **1946** Paul Erdős asked how many pairs of points among n points in the plane can be exactly **distance 1** apart, and conjectured that the best answer grows only slightly faster than n. In **May 2026** OpenAI announced that an internal model had found a **counterexample**. On **20 May 2026** nine mathematicians including **Noga Alon, Timothy Gowers, Jacob Tsimerman** and **Melanie Matchett Wood** posted a short human-verified version, noting it rests on ideas from algebraic number theory linked to **Ellenberg-Venkatesh** and **Golod-Shafarevich**. Months earlier, in **October 2025**, an AI lab's claim to have solved ten Erdős problems was walked back when they turned out to be already solved in the literature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the first famous open conjectures settled with a machine-found idea.
spotlights.memory_hook: The machine found the counterexample; nine humans checked it.

spotlights.name: Fermat's Last Theorem, checked by machine
spotlights.spot_it: Screens of Lean code, line after line of formal steps, the language where every proof is checked by software.
spotlights.story_md: **Lean** is a programming language in which a proof is accepted only if software checks every step down to the axioms. Its shared library **mathlib** holds a huge body of formal mathematics. In **2024** **Kevin Buzzard** of Imperial College London began a multi-year project to formalise Wiles's proof. On **4 September 2026**, Anthropic released a complete formalisation, about **13 million lines** of Lean written largely autonomously by Claude over **11 days**. Buzzard compiled it and confirmed the final statement matches mathlib's Fermat's Last Theorem with no extra axioms, while noting it tells us nothing mathematically new and that his project to formalise the modern proof continues.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows machine-checked proof reaching the hardest results of the 20th century.
spotlights.memory_hook: 358 years to prove, 11 days to check.

spotlights.name: Hong Wang, the Kakeya conjecture and the 2026 Fields Medals
spotlights.when: Kakeya proof February 2025; Fields Medal July 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A gold medal showing Archimedes in profile, awarded in Philadelphia in July 2026.
spotlights.story_md: In **1917** **Soichi Kakeya** asked for the smallest region in which a needle can be turned all the way round. Smaller and smaller shapes kept turning up, and the deep question became how small such sets can be in a precise dimension sense. In **February 2025** **Hong Wang** and **Joshua Zahl** posted a **127-page** proof that in three dimensions such sets must be full-dimensional. Wang, born in **1991** in Guilin, had been placed in **earth science** at Peking University before switching to mathematics. In **July 2026** in **Philadelphia** she won the **Fields Medal**, the third woman to do so, with **Yu Deng, John Pardon** and **Jacob Tsimerman**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that big human breakthroughs still drive the field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Turning a needle, settled in three dimensions.

spotlights.name: The fifth busy beaver
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny program with five states that runs for exactly 47,176,870 steps and then stops.
spotlights.story_md: The **busy beaver** question asks: among all Turing machines with n states, which runs longest before halting? Turing showed no general method can answer such questions, so each value is a fight. BB(4) was settled in 1983 at **107 steps**. In **2024** an online collaboration of mostly amateur mathematicians, **bbchallenge**, proved that **BB(5) = 47,176,870**, checking every one of millions of candidate machines and verifying the result in the **Coq (now Rocq)** proof assistant. BB(6) is beyond reach: one six-state machine halts only if a number sequence behaves in a way linked to unsolved Collatz-like problems.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Turing's limits are real, and amateurs plus computers can still push them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five states, 47 million steps, then silence.

sections.title: Recap: what mathematics is, and why it works
sections.intro_md:
**What it is.** The study of patterns and structures that follow from stated rules, checked by **proof**. Once correctly proved, a theorem stays true.

**Where it came from.** Counting and measuring: notched bones, Babylonian base 60, Egyptian fractions, Inca knots. Greece added proof. **India** added the decimal place-value system with **zero as a number** (Brahmagupta, 628), infinite series in Kerala, and Ramanujan. Baghdad passed it on and gave us **algebra** and **algorithm**; Fibonacci brought the numerals to Europe in 1202.

**How it works.** Axioms, definitions, proofs: direct, contradiction, induction, construction, and now computer checking.

**Its limits.** Cantor's bigger infinities, Russell's paradox, **Gödel's incompleteness** (1931) and **Turing's halting problem** (1936): some truths cannot be proved, some questions cannot be decided.

**Why it works.** Nobody fully knows. Maths grew from the world, symmetry ties it to physics (Noether), we keep the structures that fit, and maybe the world is mathematical at bottom. The evidence: Neptune, the positron, GPS, RSA, CT scans.

**Now.** AI writes Olympiad proofs, found an Erdős counterexample, and formalised Fermat; humans still win Fields Medals for new ideas.
