best_facts.fact: In 1846 Le Verrier found Neptune by calculation alone; Galle looked where he said and found it in under an hour, less than a degree from the predicted spot.
On 4 September 2026 a complete Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, about 13 million lines, was released after Claude worked on it largely autonomously for 11 days.
best_facts.why_surprising: 358 years to prove, 11 days to machine-check.

best_facts.fact: Smash a big block into a small one by a wall: with a mass ratio of 10,000 there are exactly 314 collisions, and a ratio of a million gives 3,141.
best_facts.why_surprising: Pi appears in a problem with no circle in sight.

best_facts.fact: A Babylonian student's tablet from about 1800 to 1600 BCE gives the square root of 2 correct to about six decimal places.
best_facts.why_surprising: Classroom work at a precision no other ancient source matches.

best_facts.fact: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day because of relativity; uncorrected, your position would drift by about 11 km a day.
best_facts.why_surprising: Einstein's curved geometry is inside every phone map.

best_facts.fact: Kerala's Madhava found the infinite series for pi around 1400 and used corrections to get 11 correct decimal places, about 250 years before Europe found the same series.
best_facts.why_surprising: Calculus-style mathematics in India before Columbus sailed.

best_facts.fact: In Principia Mathematica (1910), the proposition from which 1 + 1 = 2 follows arrives on page 379, and the finished proof is called 'occasionally useful'.
best_facts.why_surprising: The simplest sum hides hundreds of pages of logic.

best_facts.fact: Archimedes' only surviving account of how he found volumes was scraped off and overwritten as a prayer book in 1229, and recovered with imaging after a $2 million sale in 1998.
best_facts.why_surprising: Near-calculus, hidden under prayers for 700 years.

best_facts.fact: Clever Hans, the counting horse, was right 89% of the time when he could see a questioner who knew the answer, and 6% when he could not.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'maths' was in the humans' body language.

best_facts.fact: Honeybees trained to pick 'fewer' shapes placed an empty card below one shape, treating nothing as a quantity.
best_facts.why_surprising: A brain of under a million neurons ranks zero.

side_dish.title: Benford's law: how first digits catch fraud
side_dish.body_md:
Open a list of real numbers from life: river lengths, town populations, company expenses, electricity bills. Count how many start with 1. You might expect one in nine. In fact it is about **30%**. Numbers starting with 2 come next at about 18%, and only about **4.6%** start with 9.

This pattern is called **Benford's law**, after the physicist Frank Benford, who tested it on more than 20,000 numbers in 1938. The astronomer Simon Newcomb had spotted it in 1881, because the early pages of his book of logarithm tables were more worn than the later ones.

Why? Many real quantities grow by multiplying, not adding. A town of 1,000 people must double to reach 2,000, but going from 9,000 to 10,000 is only an 11% rise. So numbers spend longer with a leading 1. The law works best for data that spans several orders of magnitude.

It has a practical use. People who invent numbers tend to spread first digits too evenly. Forensic accountants and tax authorities run Benford tests to flag suspicious ledgers, and researchers use it to check election and scientific data, carefully, since some honest data does not follow it. It is a neat example of today's theme: a pattern found in pure mathematics turns up in your electricity bill and in courtrooms.

offline_task.title: Find 6174 and prove the primes go on forever
offline_task.body_md:
Two ten-minute experiments with paper and pencil.

**1. Kaprekar's routine.** Pick any four-digit number with at least two different digits, for example your birth year or the last four digits of a phone number. Arrange the digits from largest to smallest, then smallest to largest, and subtract. Repeat with the answer (keep leading zeros, so 999 is 0999). Count the steps until you hit **6174**. Try three numbers. It never takes more than seven.

**2. Euclid's proof, by hand.** Take the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7. Multiply them and add 1: you get 211. Is 211 divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7? No, it always leaves remainder 1. So either 211 is prime, or it has a prime factor not on your list. Now try 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 11 x 13 + 1 = 30,031. It is not prime: 30,031 = 59 x 509. But 59 and 509 are both new primes. Write the argument in three sentences in your own words. You have just done what Euclid did 2,300 years ago.
